title: Job Answers His Know-It-All Friends
overview: Job mocks his friends' claim to wisdom, says the world plainly does not reward good and punish bad the way they insist, and describes a God whose power topples even the strongest people and nations.

parts.label: You think you're so wise (vv. 1-3)
parts.note: Job answers with sarcasm, as if wisdom will die when his friends do. He says what they have told him is common knowledge, and he understands it as well as they do.

parts.label: Laughed at while innocent (vv. 4-6)
parts.note: Job feels mocked by friends who are comfortable while he suffers, and says people at ease look down on those who are slipping. He points out that robbers often live safe and secure, which undercuts his friends' claim that wrongdoing always brings ruin.

parts.label: Ask the animals (vv. 7-10)
parts.note: Job says all of nature shows that the LORD's hand is behind everything, holding the life of every creature. Many interpreters think his point includes the hard part: in nature the violent often thrive too, and that is also under God's hand.

parts.label: Weighing old sayings (vv. 11-12)
parts.note: Just as the tongue tastes food and keeps what it likes, the ear tests words and keeps what rings true. His friends had appealed to the wisdom of the old, and Job seems to say he can weigh those same sayings for himself; scholars are unsure whether verse 12 is sincere or ironic.

parts.label: God's overwhelming power (vv. 13-16)
parts.note: Job says true wisdom and power belong to God, who tears down what no one can rebuild and sends drought or flood at will. Even the person who deceives and the one who is fooled both stand under God's control.

parts.label: The mighty brought low (vv. 17-25)
parts.note: Rulers, judges, priests, advisers and whole nations are stripped, confused and overturned, and kings who once bound others end up bound like captives. The text does not say plainly whether Job lists this in awe or in protest, and readers hear it both ways.

disagreement: Readers differ on whether Job's long description of God's power is reverent praise or a bitter protest that this power looks arbitrary, and the book's ending, where God says Job spoke rightly, keeps the question open.
think: Have you ever been given advice that sounded wise but missed what you were actually going through, and what made it miss?
